text: If you're just starting outbound and your reply rates are low, maybe even close to zero, this video is for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As the founder of my company, One Schema, I personally generated and closed millions of dollars in revenue through founder-led sales.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As a visiting partner at YC, I've helped hundreds of YC companies improve their outbound.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in this video, we're going to cover eight things that you can do to improve your sales outreach.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Tip number one, you want to start manual before you automate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The biggest mistake I often see founders make, they'll come to me during office hours and they'll show me their email pipeline and it will all be automated.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They've loaded up a tool, they blasted out a thousand emails, and they ended up getting zero replies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The biggest issue with this is if you get zero replies from a campaign that you didn't give any thought to in the first place, then at the end, when you have zero replies, you've learned nothing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The problem could be your messaging or your company targeting, your prospect selection, your deliverability, or your subject line.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So my recommendation is to do at least 100 outreaches by hand before you automate anything.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's honestly probably going to end up being more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when I say by hand, I mean genuinely by hand.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Spend time thinking about one individual person.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What is her problem specifically?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What would actually capture her attention?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Visit her LinkedIn page and read about her company.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Doing this homework personally is how you'll come up with your highest converting outbound ideas.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Tip number two.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Targeting beats perfect messaging.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I often see founders spending hours tweaking their email copy, but they barely even think about who they're emailing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Outbound prospecting is kind of like looking for a needle in a haystack.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need a person that has the exact pain point that you solve or a perfectly crafted message won't even land.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So here's an example.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I worked with a company in the winter batch who was selling an infrastructure product that should have been sold to senior engineering leaders.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But when I opened up his LinkedIn and looked at the prospects that he was selling to, a lot of them were DevRel managers, GTM managers, there was even a customer success manager.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: He was sending hundreds of these messages and was wondering why he wasn't getting any replies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if you spend a little bit more time thinking about whether or not the person you're sending the email to actually has the pain point, you'll often end up seeing a huge increase in your reply rates.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Those wrong job titles were never going to buy, no matter how good your email was.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So how do you find the right job titles?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first thing that I typically like to do is look at the customers that you already have.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then look at the sales process.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who is the person who is pushing the last deal to close?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who actually signed the contract?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who is the person who paid?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Look at all of their job titles and then reach out to people who have similar profiles.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You should also look at who has already replied to your outbound.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if you're at the very earliest stages of your journey and you don't have any customers or any replies yet, ask yourself who in the organization has the most to gain from buying your software.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's an example.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Imagine you're selling software that monitors employee devices for security purposes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A chief security officer might get fired if there's a data breach, so they would really be interested in something like this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored at all, so they're not a great person to target.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's also really important to make sure that you're reaching out to the right companies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One mistake I'll often see companies make is they'll do a search in a tool like Sales Navigator, and it will return a bunch of profiles that maybe sort of match what they were looking for, but were actually the wrong type of company.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, if you search for tech companies in LinkedIn Sales Navigator, you're often going to get a bunch of IT implementation consultancies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you want to be really thoughtful about how you're using list building tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Verify individually that each company is a good fit for your customer or your message is going to fall on deaf ears.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As you do more outbound, you'll start to discover clues about a company that indicate that they need your product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These are called intent signals.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A great place to look is often at job postings, as they'll tell you a lot about a company's priorities.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Company growth is another very common intent signal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Imagine you're building compensation planning software.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Companies below 100 employees probably aren't introducing levels for their employees, so they won't need your software.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Companies above 500 probably already have compensation bands set.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So when they're crossing somewhere in that 100 employee range, that's a great intent signal that they need your product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every product has signals like this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your job is to discover yours.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One more thing on targeting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For closing your very first customers, it's also far easier to start with your warm network.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You really want to shake the tree to make sure you hit everyone you know because the conversion rates will be much, much higher.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Start with your personal warm network and then ask for interest from friends, families, investors, your college roommate, a guy you met at a cafe, truly whoever you can think of.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Tip number three, craft a message worth reading.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The single most important thing you can do in your email is to give a crisp explanation of how you can help the person that you're emailing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Think about the top three things that keep your buyer up at night.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What would get them fired?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What would get them promoted?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Why should they believe that you can actually help them?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When you write an email and the buyer thinks, that's exactly the problem that I have, they really get it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're likely to take the call even without fully understanding or trusting your solution.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The truth is that executives don't care about your product features.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They don't care that you have blazing fast uploads.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They don't care that your database is built in Rust.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're worried about how they're going to hit their quarterly target.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For the product explanation, I would try to make it just one sentence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You don't want to spend paragraphs and paragraphs of details here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's typically what the first call is for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You want to make sure that you establish credibility that you're the right person to help.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two common ways to do this are first to list the names of other impressive companies that you're helping, or if you don't have that yet, talk about your very relevant background for solving this problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At the end of your email, you want to include a very specific call to action.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It should be something like, got 20 minutes to hop on a call this week?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Not, does this sound interesting to you?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You want to make it really easy for them to follow up with you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Last, you can include a calendar link or a few time slots that work for you, again, to make it really, really easy for them to schedule.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You want to make sure to keep your emails really short.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: People are extremely busy and they're going to skim your emails.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every filler word that you use dilutes the ones that matter.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As a rough guide, five to eight sentences is good for email, no more than two to five for LinkedIn.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Longer than that, you should probably cut something.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's an example of an email that I think is really good.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's from the founder of Apten, which is a YC company in the S24 batch.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here are some things I really like about this email.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, notice that it's written in a really informal tone that makes him sound like a peer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: He's not using any jargon.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: He's not trying to sound super impressive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is an email that could have come from his friend.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next thing I like about this is that he establishes credibility by showing that he solved the same problem at a previous reputable company.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is that first line.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I used to be a software engineer at Tesla.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We got crazy good at using SMS to convert the people who visited our website into car buyers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next thing I like about this email is that it has a very clear call to action.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At the end, he says, would you be open to an experiment to see if we could improve your conversion rate by using AI to reactivate leads?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As the buyer, I'm thinking, okay, is this something that I would want to experiment with?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it makes it really easy for me to directly follow up with him.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The email also feels personalized to Sumir's company by mentioning that he noticed on their website that they collect phone numbers in the signup process.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And notice, he barely spends any time in the email at all explaining how this product works.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: He focuses exclusively on how he's going to help Sumir solve his problems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: After you write a great message, focus on your subject line.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You should also pay attention to the first 20 to 30 characters of the body of your email because that's what shows up in the Gmail preview.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Experimentation is the best way to come up with great subject lines.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I find that creative and kind of weird ones can end up being the winners.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, I worked with a company selling an OpenClaw-style agent product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The subject line, broken agents, performed a lot better than the more descriptive but less interesting, better agents for every workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Tip number four, improve your LinkedIn profile.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If email has subject lines, LinkedIn has your profile.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's how people decide whether or not to accept your connections and to reply.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here are a few quick tips for making sure that your profile is great.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first one is you want to make sure that you have a profile picture.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It will really increase your trust level and show your prospect that you're actually a real person.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second is you should turn that banner on the top of your LinkedIn page into an ad for your company.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Typically, it should have a really clear and concise explanation of what your company does.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Make sure that you avoid jargon here as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The third is you should rewrite your one-line description and your about section for your company into short, concise descriptions of what your company does, similar to what you put in your banner.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And fourth, elevate anything in your profile that a buyer would care about, like relevant, impressive experience, by cutting everything else that's irrelevant.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you have this really long about section that talks a lot about your hobbies and other interests and things that aren't relevant, your buyers are less likely to see the ways that you can help them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another area to invest for LinkedIn is building up your number of mutual connections.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The number of shared contacts is the single biggest predictor of whether or not somebody is going to accept your connection request in the first place.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you should focus on building relevant mutual connections with your target audience because often people within the same customer profile are connected to each other.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This takes time, so you should make it a daily habit to max out your connection allowance.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Tip number five, know what your reply rates are telling you.

text: At first, your reply rates might be very, very low.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But that's okay.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As long as you're getting a few replies, you have a baseline to improve on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Even just two to three replies on 100 emails is a great place to start iterating.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If I'm working with a founder that has on the order of two to three replies on 100 emails, here's typically the order I'll start debugging their outbound.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, I'll make sure that they're contacting the right person.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, I'll make sure that they're contacting the right companies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Third, I'll make sure that their subject lines are good.

text: So for example, make sure their website looks good and their LinkedIn profile looks good.

text: And then finally, I'll look at deliverability.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you go through all six of these areas and they all seem to be reasonable and you're still getting zero replies, this often might be indicative of a deeper product market fit issue.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Tip number six, follow up and when they reply, reply fast.

text: You never want to just send one email because it's very, very possible that the person simply just missed it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I typically like to follow up two to four times spaced out by a couple of days.

text: But the last email that I send a prospect, I often send what's called a breakup message.

text: Just let me know and I can spare your inbox.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Reply rates I find are much higher on these breakup emails because it makes them really low pressure for them to say no.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A real no is actually very useful to you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In aggregate, the many no's improve who you target in the future.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Once you get a reply, you should be like a heat seeking missile and that nothing is going to get between you and getting onto their calendar.

text: Tip number seven, block out time for outbound.

text: This is actually one of the biggest mistakes that I see founders make.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When you're a founder, there are going to be so many things competing for your attention.

text: Tip number eight, use the messaging from your customers.

text: The best feedback on your messaging always comes from your customer, not a friend, not an advisor, and not your co-founder.
